entries.name: node_1_1-accept#0
entries.script: [N1] `Xor(Coll[Byte](1), Coll[Byte](2))` — **cost 22**, the node's floor: one item, one chunk. The baseline every other node row is read against. **SEPARATING** only in the sense that a wrong BASE moves it; sigma-rust matches this row.

entries.name: node_128_128-accept#1
entries.script: [N2] 128 bytes against 128 — **still 22.** The chunk is 128 wide, so everything from 1 to 128 items costs the same. This is the row that makes N3 a boundary rather than a slope.

entries.name: node_129_129-accept#2
entries.script: [N3] 129 against 129 — **24.** The second chunk costs 2. With N2 this pins both the chunk WIDTH (128) and the per-chunk price (2), which is what `PerItemCost(10, 2, 128)` means in practice. **SEPARATING:** an implementation charging a flat cost cannot produce 24 here.

entries.name: node_129_left_1_right-accept#3
entries.script: [N4] 129 bytes on the LEFT, 1 on the right — **22, not 24.** `xorWithCosting` charges on `min(ls.length, rs.length)`, so the long operand is free. **THE SEPARATING ROW of the node half:** sigma-rust charges 24 here, i.e. on the left operand's length — a 2-cost divergence on a row where the values agree, which is the kind that survives every value test.

entries.name: node_1_left_129_right-accept#4
entries.script: [N5] The mirror: 1 on the left, 129 on the right — **22.** Its pair with N4 is the whole point: both orders cost the same on the JVM, so an implementation that reads either operand's own length gets exactly one of the two wrong. sigma-rust already matches THIS one, which is what localises its fault to the choice of operand rather than to the costing.

entries.name: method_1_1-accept#5
entries.script: [M1] `Global.xor(Coll[Byte](1), Coll[Byte](2))` as the METHOD — **cost 31. THE CORPUS'S FIRST `Global.xor` METHOD ROW**; everything before this was the `Xor` node. The 9 over N1 is the MethodCall's own cost. **SEPARATING:** sigma-rust charges 29, a flat base that is 2 low.

entries.name: method_128_128-accept#6
entries.script: [M2] 128 against 128 through the method — **31**, the same chunk width as the node.

entries.name: method_129_129-accept#7
entries.script: [M3] 129 against 129 — **33.** The method charges the SAME per-chunk 2 as the node, so a fixed method cost is right only while the shorter operand stays inside one chunk. **THE SEPARATING ROW of the method half:** sigma-rust's fixed 10 cannot reach 33.

entries.name: method_129_left_1_right-accept#8
entries.script: [M4] 129 on the left, 1 on the right, through the method — **31.** The method charges on the shorter operand too, so the node's rule is not the node's alone. **SEPARATING** (29).

entries.name: method_1_left_129_right-accept#9
entries.script: [M5] The mirror — **31**. With M4 it pins the method's symmetry the way N4/N5 pin the node's. **SEPARATING** (29).
